questionText: Under which designation was the EU AI Act published in the Official Journal?

answerOptions.text: Directive (EU) 2024/1689
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
Regulation (EU) 2023/1689
Directive (EU) 2025/1689

explanation: The EU AI Act is officially Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. A regulation is directly applicable in every Member State; a directive must first be transposed into national law.

questionText: Since when has Article 4 on AI literacy been applicable?

answerOptions.text: Since 1 August 2024
Since 2 February 2025
Since 2 August 2025
From 2 August 2026

explanation: Art. 113 point (a) makes Art. 4 and the prohibitions in Art. 5 applicable from 2 February 2025. The Commission FAQ identifies 2 August 2026 as the start of national supervision and enforcement of Art. 4. This does not automatically mean that the same fine applies to every infringement. (Source: claimId ai-literacy-supervision-2026-08-02)

questionText: A German SME uses Microsoft Copilot. Which role does it have under Art. 3?

answerOptions.text: Provider, because it uses AI in the organisation
Deployer, because it uses a finished AI system under its own authority
Distributor, because it distributes Microsoft licences
Importer, because the AI comes from the United States

explanation: Under Art. 3(4), a deployer is a person that uses an AI system under its authority. The provider is the producer, in this case Microsoft, not the user. An SME is almost always a deployer.

questionText: A US SaaS provider sells its AI platform to a company in Berlin. Does the EU AI Act apply to the US provider?

answerOptions.text: No. US companies are outside its scope
Only if it has an EU subsidiary
Yes. Under Art. 2(1)(a), the Regulation also covers providers from third countries that place AI systems on the EU market
Only for high-risk systems

explanation: The extraterritorial scope covers providers and deployers from third countries through two triggers: Art. 2(1)(a), when an AI system is placed on the market or put into service in the EU, and Art. 2(1)(c), when the output produced by the AI system is used in the EU. Block 1 L3 emphasises point (c) because it is the more common case with foreign SaaS providers: the provider sits in the United States, the output lands with a user in Germany. Location and nationality of the provider are irrelevant; either trigger establishes the Regulation's applicability independently.

questionText: How many prohibited AI practices are listed in Article 5 of the AI Act?
explanation: Art. 5(1), points (a) to (h), lists eight prohibited practices. Among them social scoring, manipulative techniques, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, and emotion recognition in the workplace.

questionText: An SME introduces an AI tool to screen job applications. Which risk class applies?

answerOptions.text: Minimal risk, because HR is not a critical area
Limited risk with a transparency obligation only
High-risk under Annex III, point 4(a)
Prohibited under Art. 5

explanation: Annex III, point 4(a), classifies AI systems intended for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular systems that evaluate applications, as high-risk. Every high-risk obligation in Chapter III, Section 2 then applies.

questionText: Which risk class applies to a conventional email spam filter under the EU AI Act?

answerOptions.text: High-risk
Limited risk
Minimal risk
Prohibited

explanation: Spam filters fall under neither Annex I nor Annex III and do not trigger a transparency obligation under Art. 50. They are therefore minimal-risk systems. Only the voluntary codes of conduct under Art. 95 apply.

questionText: A company plans to use AI to infer employees' emotions during video calls. Is this permitted?

answerOptions.text: Yes, with the employees' consent
Yes, if the works council agrees
No. It is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(f)
Yes, as a high-risk system with a conformity assessment

explanation: Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits the use of emotion-recognition systems in the workplace and in educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. Employee consent or works-council approval does not remove the prohibition.

questionText: What does Article 50 require for a publicly accessible chatbot on your website?

answerOptions.text: A conformity assessment by a notified body
A notice that the user is interacting with an AI system
CE marking on the homepage
A report to the Federal Network Agency

explanation: Art. 50(1) requires providers to design chatbots so that users are clearly informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious. The information must be clear, distinguishable and accessible.

questionText: What is the minimum retention period for the automatically generated logs of a high-risk AI system?

answerOptions.text: 30 days
3 months
6 months
10 years

explanation: Art. 19(1) requires providers to retain automatically generated logs for at least 6 months, unless applicable Union or national law requires a longer period. Art. 26(6) establishes the corresponding rule for deployers.

questionText: Which Article sets the requirements for training, validation and testing data used by high-risk AI systems?

answerOptions.text: Art. 9
Art. 10
Art. 13
Art. 26

explanation: Art. 10 requires appropriate data-governance practices for high-risk systems and data sets that are relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete. Art. 9 governs the risk-management system; Art. 13 concerns transparency towards deployers.

questionText: A high-risk system under Annex III, point 4, for selecting job applicants is to be placed on the market. Which conformity-assessment route applies?

answerOptions.text: Only assessment by a notified body under Annex VII
Internal control under Annex VI (Art. 43(2)); a notified body is not provided for
Authorisation by the Federal Network Agency
No conformity-assessment procedure is required

explanation: Art. 43(2) requires systems listed in Annex III, points 2 to 8, including point 4 on applicant selection, to follow the internal-control procedure in Annex VI; a notified body is not provided for here. Only for biometric systems listed in Annex III, point 1, does the route under Art. 43(1) depend on whether harmonised standards have been applied in full: Annex VI if they have, otherwise Annex VII with a notified body.

questionText: Which item does NOT belong in the technical documentation required by Annex IV?

answerOptions.text: A general description of the AI system, including its intended purpose
A description of the system's elements and development process
Information about monitoring, functioning and control
The provider's quarterly income statement

explanation: Annex IV lists nine categories of information, including the system description, development process, monitoring, performance metrics, risk-management system and changes. The provider's financial reports are not part of the technical documentation.

questionText: Which marking is mandatory before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market?

answerOptions.text: TÜV mark
CE marking
BSI IT-Grundschutz certificate
GDPR compliance mark

explanation: Art. 48 requires CE marking for high-risk AI systems. It records that the provider has completed the conformity assessment under Art. 43 and drawn up the EU declaration of conformity.

questionText: Above which cumulative amount of training compute is a GPAI model presumed to have systemic risk?

answerOptions.text: 10^22 FLOP
10^23 FLOP
10^25 FLOP
10^27 FLOP

explanation: Art. 51(2) sets the threshold at 10^25 floating-point operations. The Commission may adjust that figure through delegated acts. Models in the GPT-4, Claude 3 and Gemini Ultra capability class are above it.

questionText: Article 4 establishes an organisational duty concerning AI literacy. To whom is that duty primarily addressed?

answerOptions.text: Only providers of high-risk systems
Providers and deployers of AI systems, as an organisational duty
Individual employees who use AI
IT departments in organisations with more than 250 employees

explanation: Art. 4(1) addresses providers and deployers as organisations. They must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, while considering the context named in the provision. Since Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, they do not have to guarantee that each person reaches a particular level of proficiency.

questionText: When did the European Commission publish the final version of the GPAI Code of Practice?

answerOptions.text: December 2024
May 2025
10 July 2025
2 August 2026

explanation: The AI Office published the GPAI Code of Practice on 10 July 2025. Signatories such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Mistral may use adherence to the Code as a means of demonstrating compliance (Art. 53(4), Art. 55(2)), but this does not create a presumption of conformity in the legal sense. Harmonised standards under Art. 40 and 41 would create a presumption of conformity; the Code does not. (Source: AI Office, GPAI Code of Practice, 10 July 2025; Art. 53(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

questionText: Which obligation applies to you as a deployer when you use a generative AI tool to produce marketing copy for your website?

answerOptions.text: None. Deployers have no transparency obligations
Under Art. 50(4), AI-generated text must be disclosed as such when it is published to inform the public on matters of public interest
You must carry out a conformity assessment
You must place CE marking on every page

explanation: Art. 50(4) requires deployers using an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest to disclose that the text was artificially generated or manipulated, unless the content has undergone human review or editorial control. Ordinary product marketing falls within this rule only in limited circumstances.

questionText: What is the highest fine tier under Art. 99 for prohibited practices?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover
Up to EUR 50 million or 10% of annual turnover

explanation: Art. 99(3) provides for fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for infringements of Art. 5 on prohibited practices, whichever is higher. The tiers for other infringements are 3% and 1%, respectively.

questionText: Which authority does the KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, designate as the single point of contact?

answerOptions.text: Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
Federal Network Agency (BNetzA)
Federal Cartel Office
Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action

explanation: The KI-MIG has been in force since 29 July 2026. It makes the Federal Network Agency the market-surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints body for the AI Act, unless a sectoral authority is responsible. The specific complaints route is on the official Federal Network Agency website.

questionText: Within what period must a provider report a serious incident under the general rule?

answerOptions.text: Immediately and no later than 24 hours
Immediately and no later than 15 days after becoming aware of it
Within 3 months
Annually as part of post-market monitoring

explanation: Art. 73(2) requires serious incidents to be reported immediately and no later than 15 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of them. The period is reduced to 10 days in the event of death and to 2 days for widespread infringements or serious incidents involving critical infrastructure.

questionText: Who may lodge a complaint about an alleged infringement of the AI Act under Art. 85?

answerOptions.text: Only people directly affected
Only competitors and consumer organisations
Any natural or legal person
Only through a lawyer who supplies proof of authority

explanation: Art. 85 gives any natural or legal person the right to lodge a complaint with the relevant market-surveillance authority. Being directly affected is not required. The authority assesses the complaint and decides how to proceed.

questionText: A private SME uses an AI-powered CV-screening tool, which is high-risk under Annex III, point 4. Must it perform a fundamental-rights impact assessment under Art. 27?

answerOptions.text: Yes, for every high-risk system
Yes, once it processes more than 100 applications per year
No. Art. 27 applies only to public bodies and to systems under Annex III, points 5(b) and 5(c)
No, because CV screening is not a high-risk use

explanation: Art. 27(1) limits the fundamental-rights impact assessment to deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and to deployers of systems listed in Annex III, points 5(b) and 5(c). A private HR use listed under point 4 is outside that scope. A data protection impact assessment under GDPR Art. 35 must be considered separately; it is required only where the processing is likely to result in a high risk.

questionText: Which GDPR Article is the central bridge to risk work under the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: GDPR Art. 6 on lawfulness of processing
GDPR Art. 32 on security of processing
GDPR Art. 35 on data protection impact assessments
GDPR Art. 44 on transfers to third countries

explanation: AI Act Art. 26(9) expressly refers to the data protection impact assessment under GDPR Art. 35. Deployers of high-risk systems can use existing DPIAs as a basis and add AI-specific matters such as training data, human oversight and logging.

questionText: What is the first step in a five-step AI Act audit for an SME?

answerOptions.text: Commission a conformity assessment
Create an AI inventory covering every AI system used in the organisation
Apply for CE marking
Perform a data protection impact assessment

explanation: No inventory, no classification. No classification, no way to name the obligations that apply. Step 1 is a complete AI inventory covering provider, purpose and data flows. Risk classification, documentation, gap analysis and remediation come after that.

questionText: You interact with a support chatbot. From when must the AI interaction generally be apparent under Art. 50(1)?

answerOptions.text: From 2 August 2026, before or when the interaction starts (Art. 50(1))
From 2 February 2025, if the chatbot system is registered
Only from 2 December 2027, when the high-risk rules apply
Only for chatbots with a GPAI licence

explanation: Art. 50(1) generally requires providers to design systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, before or at the time of their first interaction, unless this is obvious. The obligation becomes applicable on 2 August 2026. (Source: Art. 50(1), Art. 113 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

questionText: Who is outside the scope of the AI Act when using AI solely for private purposes?

answerOptions.text: No one. The Regulation applies to every natural person
Natural persons using AI solely for private purposes: they are not deployers within the meaning of Art. 2(10)
Only people in countries outside the EU
Only retired people

explanation: Art. 2(10) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 expressly excludes obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal, non-professional activity. A person using ChatGPT at home for their own writing is not a deployer in the legal sense. The Regulation applies once the use takes place in a professional context.
